name: Crime & Punishment
body:
There are many crimes that a society could have in place with a number of punishments for each crime. The following crimes have punishments associated with them such as sentences of imprisonment. It is important to note that these punishments assume a human-centric society, so the prison sentences may be higher in a society populated by longer lived races or shorter in a society filled with shorter lived races. Feel free to adjust the sentences of imprisonment to best suit the society the crime was committed in. Also, do note that some crimes would have contradictory effects if applied together, such as life imprisonment and execution. If this is the case, use the harsher penalty, in this instance, execution.

In addition, there may be several crimes which increase the gold fine or sentence of imprisonment of another crime and as such, such penalties are added separately from one another if applicable. For example, if someone were sentenced 4 years in prison and a 5,000 gp fine for arson and did so with both magic and while endangering a child, the fine and sentence of imprisonment would normally be 200% the norm for child endangerment and 200% the norm for the use of magic during the course of the crime. This would lead to the fine being increased by 5,000 gp for the use of magic and by another 5,000 for child endangerment for a total of 15,000 gp. Similarly, the sentence of imprisonment would be increased by 4 years for the use of magic and another 4 years for endangering a child, leading to a prison sentence of 12 years.

Finally, you may notice that there are three different types of punishments listed: high punishment, normal punishment, and low punishment. These different types of punishment reflect not only society’s personal opinions of the crimes in question, but the judge’s own personal biases. In a society where thievery is the norm, a charge of theft might be given a low punishment, but if in the same society the theft were committed against the judge’s family, the judge would more than likely find reason to use the high punishment. Even assuming a fair trial, different punishments might be given to the same crime depending on how heinous the crime is. A person who murdered someone in a fit of passion might be given the normal punishment while someone who has the obvious makings of a serial killer by using a modus operandi might be given the high punishment.

List of Crimes & Punishments
Accessory to Crime

When a person is an accessory to crime, they are guilty of either having been a part of the planning stages of a crime, but not having committed the crime themselves, or they are guilty of aiding and abetting the criminal after the crime was complete. Unlike an accomplice to a crime, who would also be given the same charge, an accessory to a crime is seen as a lesser partner and so is usually given a lesser sentence.

High Punishment: Same charge as the primary criminal

Normal Punishment: 75% of the fine or prison sentence of the primary criminal

Low Punishment: 50% of the fine or prison sentence of the primary criminal

Adultery

Adultery is voluntary sexual intercourse between at least one married individual with someone who is not their lawfully wedded spouse. This crime is most often punished in societies that hold morals above all else or worship deities that preach devotion to one’s family. In some instances, this crime is paired together with breaking an oath.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: 1-4 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: 5 gold fine paid to wronged spouse and 1 week in the pillory

Animal Cruelty

Many species of animals are seen as less able to defend themselves from sapient beings than other sapients, therefore many societies make laws specifically designed to protect animals from abuse. In some cases, this includes beating them and in others it includes keeping them placed in inadequate conditions. While in most societies it is seen as acceptable to kill an animal quickly in order to prepare it for food, there are a few societies in which certain animals are protected from being killed, while in the strictest of societies, killing an animal for any purpose is illegal.

High Punishment: Life imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 1-10 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: 100 gp fine

Arson

Arson is defined as the purposeful burning of another person’s property or dwelling. Depending on whether people were harmed or killed in the act of committing arson, there may be additional charges brought up as well. Depending on whether or not the person setting the fire knew that there were people inside the dwelling that was set fire to, this could include attempted murder, murder, or manslaughter. The charge of arson without other crimes is considered property damage and thus the property must be paid for.

High Punishment: Fine of 300% the value of the property paid to victim & 10-20 years imprisonment

Normal Punishment: Fine of 200% the value of the property paid to victim & 1-10 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: Fine equal to the value of the property paid to victim

Assault and Battery

Assault is defined as the act of causing someone to fear harm from an assailant. Battery, meanwhile, refers to the actual act of causing unlawful harm to someone. These crimes are usually paired together, though in some instances can be separated. In many cases assault and battery is either the result of intoxication, such as a fight at a tavern, or due to a personal grudge against the victim. In the case of a mutual fight, it may be difficult to determine who the original assailant was and so both parties are charged.

High Punishment: Removal of the hands at the wrists

Normal Punishment: 100 gp fine paid to victim plus the cost of medical expenses

Low Punishment: Victim has the chance of inflicting the same injuries they received or sending the criminal to a pillory for 1 week

Assassination

Assassination is defined as the acceptance of goods or services in exchange for the unlawful killing of another individual or individuals. This crime is always paired with murder in the case of a successful assassination or attempted murder in the case of an unsuccessful assassination, along with any other crimes which may have been broken during the assassination. Both the assassin themselves and the person who paid for the assassination are usually charged with the crime.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: Life imprisonment

Low Punishment: 20-40 years imprisonment

Criminal Content

In the list of crimes below, you will notice several notable absences particularly surrounding the subjects of domestic abuse, sexual violence, and slavery. This was a conscious decision made in order to remain as respectful as possible to the subject matter and not gamify these topics. When engaging with a roleplaying group, there are expectations surrounding violence. This is why it is generally acceptable to have players fight enemies to the death and act against all manner of fiends and criminals.

This changes with the very real and very serious topics of domestic abuse, sexual violence, and slavery. We acknowledge that they exist but found it would be crass and inappropriate to include rules and game elements surrounding them. What you do at your table is your choice, but we encourage Game Masters to approach such subject matter with the utmost care and respect and have serious discussions with their players to see if it is even appropriate to have within your games at all.

Attempted Crime

When someone is guilty of an attempted crime, it means that they were in the process of committing the crime but were stopped in some way shape or form. For example, attempted murder is when someone is in the process of trying to unlawfully kill someone and is stopped by an external force, such as the potential victim fighting back or the city guard stopping the criminal before they kill anyone.

High Punishment: Same charge as if the crime were carried out

Normal Punishment: 75% of the fine or prison sentence as if the crime were carried out

Low Punishment: 50% of the fine or prison sentence as if the crime were carried out

Banditry

Banditry is defined as engaging in organized crime along with a group of wanted accomplices, usually outside the borders of a town or city. Depending on a bandit organization’s crimes, individual members may be wanted alive or dead. These crimes usually include vandalism, robbery, and murder. Due to the severity of the crimes and the wanted status of members of a bandit organization, there are usually laws in place protecting those who kill them when being threatened.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: Life imprisonment

Low Punishment: Paying a bounty or imprisonment proportional to the crimes committed

Blackmail

Blackmail is defined as the criminal act of threatening not to reveal damaging information about a person in exchange for monetary gain or favors. This is not to be confused with extortion in which these things are gained through threats of physical violence. An example of extortion is requesting to be paid a certain amount of gold every month in exchange for not revealing information to the public about an affair that the victim has been engaging in.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment plus a fine of 200% of whatever monetary gain was received throughout the course of the blackmail paid to the victim

Normal Punishment: A fine of 200% of whatever monetary gain was received throughout the course of the blackmail paid to the victim

Low Punishment: A fine of whatever monetary gain was received throughout the course of the blackmail paid to the victim

Blasphemy

Usually a law only applied in the most religious of societies, blasphemy is defined as speaking out against a religion’s tenets or a violation of sacred sites or rituals. This can include speaking against a servant of that religion such as a priest or other holy official or questioning their decrees openly. In most societies, though blasphemy is not illegal, there are still social stigmas associated with speaking out against a religion or holy people and other false charges may be brought up such as slander against a deity, who is usually represented by a member of their religion.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: Lashed with a whip at least 10 times and then until the criminal apologizes for their crimes

Low Punishment: 1 week in the pillory

Brandishing a Weapon

In most polite societies it is considered rude to hold an unsheathed weapon in public without a lawful reason to do so. In certain societies it is seen as menacing the citizens and so is punished accordingly. The exact law varies from region to region, so a brandished weapon may be anything from an unsheathed sword to a nocked bow or a wand held in hand.

High Punishment: 10 lashes with a whip and confiscation of the weapon

Normal Punishment: Confiscation of the weapon

Low Punishment: Confiscation of the weapon, which can be retrieved when leaving the town or city in which the law was broken

Breaking an Oath

When someone swears an oath, they are usually bound by merely their honor to uphold it with social consequences applied if the person breaks it: loss of trust, expulsion from organizations, and even friendships ended. But when someone swears an oath in front of a priest, judge, or another official and it is found that the oath was broken, the oathbreaker may be called in to face justice.

High Punishment: Stripped of any titles held and exiled

Normal Punishment: Public shaming and loss of rights to form contracts

Low Punishment: 1 week in the pillory

Bribery

When a charge of bribery is brought up, there are almost always at least two offenders, the person offering the bribe and the person being bribed (if that person actually accepts the bribe). The act of bribery is defined as offering or accepting services, monetary gain, or favors in exchange for influencing the actions of a law enforcement official, member of government, or anyone else with power over the law in exchange for that individual reciprocating with the gift with a favor that involves abusing their power.

High Punishment: All persons involved with the bribe have 50% of their total wealth confiscated, are stripped of any titles held, and 5-20 years imprisonment

Normal Punishment: All persons involved with the bribe are stripped of any titles held and 1-10 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: All persons involved with the bribe are stripped of any titles held

Burglary

Burglary is defined as the unlawful entry into a building with the intent to commit another crime. This other crime can vary between murder, robbery, or other nefarious deeds and is always paired with the crime of trespassing.

High Punishment: 1-5 years imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 100-1,000 gp fine paid to owner of the property

Low Punishment: 10-50 gp fine paid to owner of the property

Child Endangerment

Children are amongst the most vulnerable in society and thus crimes that affect them or put them in any form of danger are seen as especially heinous. In most jurisdictions, children are protected under the law under the assumption that they cannot protect themselves. Thus, penalties for endangering children are quite severe. More appropriately though, child endangerment can also refer to the crime of a child’s guardian putting them in a dangerous situation that could have been avoided if not for negligence. These two different definitions tend to have separate charges associated with them.

High Punishment: Loss of custody and 5-10 years imprisonment or 400% of the fine or prison sentence if a separate crime affected a child

Normal Punishment: Loss of custody and 1-5 years imprisonment or 200% of the fine or prison sentence if a separate crime affected a child

Low Punishment: Loss of custody or 150% of the fine or prison sentence if a separate crime affected a child

Consorting with Fiends

Whether they be devils, demons, or some other sort of evil entity, fiends are widely considered dangerous and with no redeeming qualities whatsoever, with those who consort with them being labeled diabolists and demoniacs. Only the evilest societies do not have any laws against making deals with fiends of any sort or keeping them in one’s employ. Even being seen conversing with a fiend is enough for arrest in some jurisdictions, let alone summoning or binding them. In some jurisdictions, this also applies to speaking their languages: Abyssal or Infernal.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: Life imprisonment

Low Punishment: Exile

Conspiracy

Sometimes conflated with an attempted crime, conspiracy is the act of two or more people gathering together and organizing a crime with intent to commit it at a later date, but being apprehended before the crime could take place. This subtle distinction allows law enforcement officers such as guards and inquisitors to arrest someone even when a crime has not yet been committed in the interest of public safety.

High Punishment: Same charge as if the crime were carried out

Normal Punishment: 75% of the fine or prison sentence as if the crime were carried out

Low Punishment: 50% of the fine or prison sentence as if the crime were carried out

Contempt of Court

Contempt is simply defined as the disruption of a trial and its proceedings or disobedience in a trial when given an order by the presiding judge. This can be a charge brought up within the courtroom itself, such as making a mockery of the judge and the proceedings, or it can happen outside of the courtroom, such as refusing to show up to a trial.

High Punishment: 10 lashes with a whip for every violation of courtroom proceedings

Normal Punishment: 1 week imprisonment and a 10 gp fine for every violation of courtroom proceedings

Low Punishment: 1 week in the pillory after the trial is over

Corruption

Corruption is a charge usually brought to the highest courts in the land. It is defined as an official abusing their official capacities as members of law enforcement, government, or nobility in order to evade the legal system and unlawfully use their station to gain some sort of benefit for themselves or another person. This is differentiated from bribery in that a person charged with corruption is the initiator of the crime and procures a benefit for themselves rather than being given such a benefit by another person or group.

High Punishment: The criminal has 50% of their total wealth confiscated, is stripped of any titles held, and 5-20 years imprisonment

Normal Punishment: The criminal is stripped of any titles held and is exiled

Low Punishment: The criminal is stripped of any titles held

Counterfeiting

Counterfeiting is defined as the act of copying or imitating an item, usually with lesser quality materials, without being authorized by the proper authorities to do so, passing the copy off as a genuine article. Counterfeiting usually has a financial gain, and thus money, works of art, and more can be counterfeit. Counterfeit goods can be created through mundane means or through magic. Counterfeiting is usually paired with the charge of theft due to the sale of counterfeit goods.

High Punishment: Removal of the hands at the wrists and fine paid to the court equal to the original item’s cost

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per 100 gp cost of the counterfeit item’s original and fine paid to the court equal to the original item’s cost

Low Punishment: Fine paid to the court equal to the original item’s cost

Crime While in Possession of Magic

In societies where magic is more common, it is not surprising that some canny criminals have found ways of using it to commit crimes that would have either been harder or outright impossible without its use. For example, a mage using an invisibility spell to sneak into a highly restricted area to commit theft. As such, many societies have laws against using magic during the use of a crime, making harsher penalties for those who do. Such a charge may in fact stack with unlawful use of enchantments or divinations at times.

High Punishment: 400% of the fine or prison sentence

Normal Punishment: 200% of the fine or prison sentence

Low Punishment: 150% of the fine or prison sentence

Crime While in Possession of Weaponry

Committing a crime while in possession of a weapon is seen by the courts as intent to use that weapon whilst in the process of committing the crime and is thus looked at more seriously than a crime committed without a weapon. As such, even if the weapon was not used, it is assumed that it would have been used if given the opportunity, else why carry a weapon at all? In certain societies where carrying a weapon is the norm, this may not be a crime, or the charge may be waived entirely if it is determined that the weapon was brought along for a lawful reason.

High Punishment: 400% of the fine or prison sentence

Normal Punishment: 200% of the fine or prison sentence

Low Punishment: 150% of the fine or prison sentence

Crimes Against Life

There are certain classifications of crime that are considered so heinous that they go beyond the bounds of the normal justice system. When someone is charged with crimes against life, it is usually by a ruling monarch or the high priest of a religion. These crimes are usually a multitude of others such as a mass murder or organization or planning of a genocide. In such a case, there is usually no trial involved, merely the whims of the monarch or high priest involved deciding what sentence to give the criminal.

High Punishment: Execution followed by a revivify spell indefinitely until the presiding judge deems the punishment sufficient or funding for the revivify spell runs out

Normal Punishment: Execution

Low Punishment: Life imprisonment

Crimes Against Nobility

In some societies, the nobility is afforded more rights than the common people and thus are protected under the law against punishment or retaliation for crimes which would normally be excused were the committed by a member of the lower classes. For example, if a member of the nobility were to commit assault and battery against a peasant, instead of being able to fight back, the peasant would be charged with assault and battery themselves if they were to strike the offending noble as it is seen as only proper for the courts and presiding judge to decide what punishment nobility deserve.

High Punishment: 400% of the fine or prison sentence

Normal Punishment: 200% of the fine or prison sentence

Low Punishment: 150% of the fine or prison sentence

Desecration of the Dead

Desecration of the dead is defined as a few different acts which all fall under the same category of crime. Therefore, desecration of the dead can be anything from digging up a grave to steal the remains of the corpse that was once there to mutilating a deceased body. Special attention is paid to necromancers who must receive written permission in the form of a contract in order to animate the corpse of another individual, though in some jurisdictions this is also illegal. Scientists who receive special permission to study cadavers from the government or ruling body are typically given permission to ignore this law.

High Punishment: 5-15 years imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 1-10 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: 100 gp fine

Destruction of a Soul

The destruction of the soul is a particularly vile offense that requires the most powerful and evil of magics to accomplish, usually in a process to becoming a powerful undead such as a lich. As such, it is very difficult to even bring such people to trial, though when they are, it is done with powerful protections and the verdict is always guilty.

High Punishment: Execution followed by a revivify spell indefinitely until the presiding judge deems the punishment sufficient or funding for the revivify spell runs out

Normal Punishment: Execution followed by destruction of the remains

Low Punishment: Execution

Disturbing the Peace

Disturbing the peace is a lesser crime usually defined as making oneself obnoxious in public or engaging in rowdy behavior typically disapproved of in polite society. This can include using vulgar language, making excessive noise, or even doomsaying in a public space.

High Punishment: 1 month imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 1 week in the pillory

Low Punishment: A sincere public apology

Drug Manufacturing

The first in a wider list of crimes related to drugs. The exact definition of a drug can vary from place to place, ranging from all manner of illicit medical, herbal, or magical substances meant to be ingested. Drug manufacturing is the creation of these illicit substances for any reason without appropriate permission or licensure from the state. This crime is usually paired with a charge of drug possession.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per dose of the drug produced

Normal Punishment: 1 month imprisonment per dose of the drug produced

Low Punishment: 50 gp fine per dose of the drug produced

Drug Possession

The second in a wider list of crimes related to drugs. Drug possession is when a person is found with illicit substances. Depending on the region, drug possession can either be the ownership of said illicit substance in any quantity while in other regions criminal charges are reserved for ownership of more than a certain amount. Most communities allow for alchemists and apothecaries to have licenses which allow them to bypass these restrictions. It is not necessary for one to use these illicit substances to be charged with the crime.

High Punishment: 5 years imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment and 50 gp fine

Low Punishment: Mandatory treatment for addiction

Drug Trafficking

The last in a wider list of crimes related to drugs. Drug trafficking is differentiated from drug possession in that the trafficking charge is reserved for those who distribute or sell illicit substances. There are usually exceptions made for alchemists and apothecaries who can prescribe these normally illicit substances for medical use. This crime is usually paired with a charge of drug possession.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per dose of the drug sold

Low Punishment: 100 gp fine per dose of the drug sold

Embezzlement

Embezzlement is a financial crime committed by those left in charge of money for an organization. The crime describes when someone who was entrusted with money or property purposely stealing these assets for personal gain. This is differentiated from theft as theft refers to a person who had no right to access the organization’s assets whereas embezzlement is reserved for those who lawfully came to manage these assets before stealing them.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment for every 10 gp embezzled and repayment equal to 200% of the total embezzled

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment for every 100 gp embezzled and repayment equal to the total embezzled

Low Punishment: Fine equal to the total embezzled

Espionage

Espionage is a crime of watching and gathering information on a person or organization, usually connected to a government, and giving this information to an outside source. Given the nature of this crime it is usually punished harshly and if the person charged with espionage is a citizen of the territory they are spying on, they may also be charged separately with crimes related to treason.

High Punishment: Life imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 10 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Extortion

Extortion is a crime that describes when someone obtains money or property using threats of violence. This is distinct from blackmail in that blackmail does not threaten physical violence, but to reveal secret and private information if one is not paid monetarily or with favors. Extortion is thus usually punished more heavily than blackmail.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment for every 10 gp extorted and repayment equal to 200% of the total extorted

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment for every 100 gp embezzled and repayment equal to the total extorted

Low Punishment: Fine equal to the total extorted

False Divination

Those who pretend to be soothsayers or those true diviners who reveal false information can be charged with false divination. This is not a punished crime in certain communities as it is sometimes seen as no worse than any normal lie. In particularly spiritual or magic oriented communities, however, this crime is sometimes paired with fraud (if the divination was paid for) or even heresy (if pretending to gain visions from a deity).

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment for every false divination

Normal Punishment: 1 month imprisonment for every false divination

Low Punishment: 1 week in the pillory for every false divination

Fencing

Fencing is the crime of knowingly buying stolen goods in order to resell them to others. When reselling stolen goods, the fence usually obscures the fact that the goods were stolen in the first place, acting as a legitimate entrepreneur. Due to the cooperative nature of this crime, there are usually associated charges for stealing the goods, especially if the fence contracted the thief to steal the goods directly.

High Punishment: 5 years imprisonment and fine equal to 300% of the value of the stolen goods

Normal Punishment: 1 year’s imprisonment and fine equal to the value of the stolen goods

Low Punishment: Fine equal to the value of the stolen goods

Forbidden Knowledge

There are pieces of information that some courts would rather remain hidden. In some instances, this knowledge can be as simple as knowing state secrets. In other instances, it could be a lot more complex such as possessing information about a specific topic that can prove hazardous to others. This is most often invoked with magical secrets of particularly dangerous rituals or even knowledge of eldritch beings.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: Life imprisonment

Low Punishment: Memories of the forbidden knowledge wiped with magic

Forgery

Forgery refers to the crime of creating a false copy of something in order to pass it off as legitimate. This is a wide category of crime and can refer to any number of things, including manufacturing fake art, money, legal documents, items for sale, and more. Forgery is also used as a term to describe the alteration of legitimate documents to pass the alterations off as the original, such as changing signatures or dates on a contract.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment for every item forged and fine equal to 300% of the value of the forged goods

Normal Punishment: 1 month imprisonment for every item forged and fine equal to 150% of the value of the forged goods

Low Punishment: Fine equal to total of forged goods

Fraud

Similar to forgery, fraud is a crime in which the culprit uses lies and deceit for financial gain. Unlike forgery, fraud generally does not involve the alteration or creation of items in order to pass them off as legitimate and as such a criminal can be charged with both fraud and forgery in certain circumstances. An example of fraud would be lying about the origin of an otherwise legitimate item in order to sell it for a higher price than it would ordinarily go for.

High Punishment: 5 years imprisonment and a fine equal to 300% of the defrauded amount

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment and a fine equal to 150% of the defrauded amount

Low Punishment: Fine equal to the defrauded amount

Gossip

Gossip refers to the casual conversation of unconfirmed rumors related to a person or organization. Gossip is not a crime in all regions and as such the exact definition may vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction and range from intentionally creating and spreading said rumors to merely entertaining them without putting a stop to the gossip. Gossip is differentiated from slander in that the rumors need not be damaging to a person, but in instances where the gossip is damaging to one’s reputation, the two crimes may be prosecuted together.

High Punishment: Removal of the tongue

Normal Punishment: 1 day in the pillory

Low Punishment: A sincere public apology

Grave Robbing

The crime of stealing a corpse or its belongings from its burial spot is nearly universal. The punishment for this crime can vary wildly depending on if it is the sole charge or if it is paired with other crimes such as desecration of the dead or theft. In instances where the act of grave robbing causes an undead to form, the criminal is usually punished for whatever crime or destruction the resulting undead causes. In communities with undead rulers, additional charges of theft or even blasphemy may be added.

High Punishment: 10 years imprisonment and 1,000 gp fine

Normal Punishment: 5 years imprisonment and 500 gp fine

Low Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Harassment

Harassment is the term used for a wide range of offenses, broadly defined as malicious and repeated interruptions in a person’s life. Though usually taking the form of threats and intimidation, harassment can be any number of behaviors which prevent a person from living in a state of general contentment. As the definitions are broad, it is usually up to each region to define what behaviors go past general annoyance and are elevated to criminal activity.

High Punishment: 5 year imprisonment and 10 lashes with a whip to be dealt by the victim

Normal Punishment: 1 month imprisonment

Low Punishment: 1 week in the stockades

Hate Crimes

Hate crimes are crimes committed against a person or person because of their belonging or perceived belonging to a social group, such as one’s race. This is a category of crime that is generally paired with others. If it is proven that a crime was committed because of these reasons, this crime is added to the charges and intensifies the punishment.

High Punishment: 400% of the fine or prison sentence

Normal Punishment: 200% of the fine or prison sentence

Low Punishment: 150% of the fine or prison sentence

Homelessness

In some particularly tyrannical societies, those who are not able to find a home are afforded fewer rights. As an incentive to get them to leave the area, homelessness is criminalized. In some areas, fines are imposed for every month one is without a home, while in other areas, those found sleeping on the streets are jailed.

High Punishment: Forced labor until a home can be purchased with accumulated wealth

Normal Punishment: 1 week imprisonment

Low Punishment: 10 gp fine until a home is purchased

Identity Theft

Identity theft is the crime of pretending to be someone else. This crime can take many forms, ranging from disguising oneself in person in order to look like another person, to falsifying one’s identity in written correspondence. Shapechangers and those gifted with the ability to use spells such as disguise self or alter self also often run afoul of the law by using their abilities to take the form of another person.

High Punishment: 1 year in jail and 500 gp fine to the victim

Normal Punishment: 1 month in the pillory and 100 gp fine to the victim

Low Punishment: A sincere public apology

Indecent Exposure

Those found with either minimal clothing or in the nude can be charged with indecent exposure. This is only a crime in public areas or where others might otherwise easily see the offender. There are usually some exceptions that are made, such as in bathhouses or during religious ceremonies.

High Punishment: Banishment from the community

Normal Punishment: 1 year in jail

Low Punishment: 1 month in the pillory

Joblessness

In some societies, perceived laziness is seen as a crime to be punished, leading to laws punishing those without work. Though laxer punishments include fines which are meant to incentivize either finding work or leaving entirely, stricter punishments may include forced labor until gainful employment is found.

High Punishment: Forced labor until other lawful employment is found

Normal Punishment: Banishment from the community until lawful employment is found

Low Punishment: 10 gp fine until lawful employment is found

Kidnapping

Kidnapping is the crime of holding someone captive by force or coercion. The harshness of the punishment for this crime is usually dependent on how long the victim was held captive and whether or not there were other crimes involved. There are sometimes exceptions made such as in the case of mercenaries or bounty hunters capturing wanted criminals in order to turn them into the proper authorities.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: 10 years imprisonment and 1,000 gp fine to the victim

Low Punishment: 10 years imprisonment

Libel/Slander

Both libel and slander refer to the crimes of spreading misinformation about a person or organization, whether knowingly or unknowingly. Unlike gossip, this misinformation must be damaging to the victim’s reputation, livelihood, or health. The difference between these two crimes is that libel is done in print (such as in a newspaper or fliers) while slander is spread through word of mouth such as in a public forum. The severity of the penalty depends on the damage caused to the victim.

High Punishment: Half of all money and property redistributed to the victim and removal of the tongue

Normal Punishment: Half of all money and property redistributed to the victim

Low Punishment: Repayment of possible damages as estimated by a judge

Littering

Littering is the crime of discarding waste or other items in a public place or other area designated as needing to be maintained. This charge can also apply when waste is left in natural places such as forests or bodies of water. This is usually punished far more heavily in communities in touch with nature such as where druids or fey hold power.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 20 gp fine

Low Punishment: 1 day in the pillory

Magic Use

Some places have outlawed the use of magic for one reason or another. This is a wide range of crimes and depending on where this crime is committed, this can refer to using any magical abilities whatsoever, specifically spells, or specific schools of magic such as enchantments or necromancy. In many locations that hold magic use to be a punishable crime, there are exceptions such as for healers, government officials, or licensed scholars such as a court wizard.

High Punishment: Removal of hands at the wrists

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per use of magic

Low Punishment: Banishment from the community

Manslaughter

Manslaughter refers to the act of accidentally killing another sentient being without meaning to do so. In most cases, a person’s direct actions must be shown to have resulted in a person’s death. For example, if two people were caught in a heated argument and one pushed another, leading them to break their neck upon landing on the ground, this would likely be considered manslaughter as though there was an intention to harm there was no intent to kill. Likewise, a person recklessly steering a horse-drawn wagon through the street and barreling over and killing a bystander would be charged with manslaughter. Once evidence that a death was intentional, this crime no longer applies, and murder is the appropriate crime.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: 20-40 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: 10 years imprisonment

Money Laundering

Money laundering is the crime of taking wealth earned through illegal or illicit means and making it appear to come from legitimate practices. This usually takes the form of funneling it into a business and misinterpreting the financial gain from those legitimate activities in order to hide the original source of the ill-gotten gains.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per 100 gp laundered

Normal Punishment: 1 month imprisonment per 100 gp laundered

Low Punishment: 1 month imprisonment per 500 gp laundered

Murder

The unlawful killing of a sentient being. This crime is distinct from manslaughter in that murder refers to a premeditated killing while manslaughter is generally accidental. Depending on the level of premeditation and the planning that went into the murder, this crime can be punished more severely. There are sometimes exceptions to this with some people being given a license to kill by the ruling body. This is usually reserved for adventurers, bounty hunters, and law enforcement.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: Life imprisonment

Low Punishment: 20-40 years imprisonment

Owning a Weapon

In some locations, the act of owning a weapon is illegal. What is defined as a weapon and what is a tool can depend on several different circumstances; for example, a longbow may be excused in a location where hunting is prevalent, but a sword would not be. There are usually some exceptions to this law such as those with a license from the ruling body or who would require it for their job, such as soldiers or city guards.

High Punishment: 10 lashes with a whip and confiscation of the weapon

Normal Punishment: Confiscation of the weapon

Low Punishment: Confiscation of the weapon, which can be retrieved when leaving the town or city in which the law was broken

Perjury

Sometimes known as oathbreaking, perjury is the crime of swearing an oath and not holding true to it. In many cases this is as simple as swearing an oath to tell the truth to a public official or religious body and lying instead. Paladins or knights who break their oaths are sometimes held to punishment by others who have sworn the same oath. Depending on the circumstances and severity of the breach, this crime is sometimes excused particularly if two oaths come in conflict, and one must be broken to uphold the greater oath.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: A period or specific act of penance chosen by the judge

Low Punishment: Public shaming

Piracy

Piracy is the crime of robbery while at sea or ocean, usually as an act committed by a group. This crime usually encompasses several others depending on how a pirate treats their victims. Given the nature of the cargo they tend to steal, most pirates are given a death sentence if caught. There are exceptions for government sanctioned piracy, as some authorities give licenses to qualified sailors to commit a legalized form of piracy known as privateering. These licenses usually note approved actions that a privateer can take, and which targets they are allowed to act against.

High Punishment: Execution

Normal Punishment: Life imprisonment

Low Punishment: Paying a bounty or imprisonment proportional to the crimes committed

Poaching

Poaching is the act of hunting and killing animals on land owned by another. This is sometimes enforced between neighboring communities to ensure that there is enough wild game to share. In other instances, peasantry can be charged with poaching for hunting on lands owned by nobility. Nobles oftentime give special permissions and licenses or restrict hunting to specific days in order to preserve their lands.

High Punishment: Removal of the hands at the wrists

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment and fine equal to the cost of the animals killed

Low Punishment: Fine equal to the cost of the animals killed

Prostitution

Prostitution is the crime of engaging in sexual activity in exchange for money. Who can be charged with this crime can vary from place to place. Some authorities will only charge the person buying sex as a service while some will charge the prostitute themselves with the crime. Depending on the location, this practice may be entirely legal so long as it is done within specific locations, usually brothels or temples dedicated to deities of passion or love.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Normal Punishment: Banishment from the community

Low Punishment: 1 week in the pillory

Public Intoxication

Public intoxication is the crime of being visibly under the influence of either drugs or alcohol while in a public space. In some locations, someone could be charged with this crime if they are anywhere except their home while under the influence of these substances but in others, there are locations and events (such as at taverns or during public festivals) where this crime either does not apply or the law keepers ignore its enforcement.

High Punishment: 1 month imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 20 gp fine

Low Punishment: Placed in a pillory until sober

Rebellion

Rebellion, one of the two crimes which make up a larger category of treason, is the act of open or violent conflict against the ruling authority of the land. In some instances, rebellions are nothing more than minor conflicts. Some are better classified as civil wars. This crime is special in that not only is the punishment usually death given the nature of what makes a rebellion, but the trial process tends to be shorter or nonexistent, with government officials sometimes being given special authority to put down rebels however they can.

High Punishment: Torture for an indefinite amount of time followed by execution

Normal Punishment: Execution

Low Punishment: Life imprisonment

Resisting Arrest

Resisting arrest is a crime which by its necessity is added onto another. Resisting arrest occurs when a legal authority is interfered with in their attempts to arrest someone, whether this means the suspect fights against the attempt for officers of the law to detain them or actively flees any pursuit.

High Punishment: 400% of the fine or prison sentence

Normal Punishment: 200% of the fine or prison sentence

Low Punishment: 150% of the fine or prison sentence

Robbery

Robbery is the act of stealing money or property through threats or acts of violence. This is a crime usually kept separate from theft which usually assumes no threats of violence are made.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per 100 gp worth of goods stolen and a fine equal to 200% the value of those goods

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per 100 gp worth of goods stolen and a fine equal to the total value of those goods

Low Punishment: A fine equal to the value of the stolen goods

Sedition

Sedition, one of the two crimes which make up a larger category of treason, is the crime of organization or activism which leads a country towards rebellion. Depending on the laws in place and how strict the lawmakers in the country are, such action may be anything as simple as speaking out against the policies set by the ruling authority or as dire as starting armed conflict. As the threshold depends on the country, so does the punishment with some countries having a minimum sentence of imprisonment and while the maximum sentence usually ensures no one attempts such action ever again.

High Punishment: Public torture and execution

Normal Punishment: Life imprisonment

Low Punishment: Banishment from the nation

Smuggling

Smuggling is the crime of illegally bringing goods into or out of a territory, especially by avoiding normal legal means. This is usually to avoid having contraband confiscated and to avoid tariffs or other fees which legal routes may necessitate. The punishment is usually dependent on the type of goods being smuggled, with weapons, illicit substances, magic items, and even people being typical items to be smuggled.

High Punishment: Removal of the hands at the wrists and 5 years imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 2 years imprisonment

Low Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Solicitation

Solicitation is the crime of trying to convince another to commit a separate crime. In most cases, the solicitor would face the same punishment as the person committing the crime.

High Punishment: Same charge as the crime they solicited

Normal Punishment: 75% of the fine or prison sentence of the solicited crime

Low Punishment: 50% of the fine or prison sentence of the solicited crime

Stalking

Stalking is the crime of unwanted surveillance of or communication with a person. Stalking usually happens on multiple occasions and can only be classified as such if a pattern emerges. The breadth of this crime is wide and so different jurisdictions will have different standards as to what defines stalking. In some places, intent to cause harm must be proven. In other cases simply showing this unwanted behavior has been repeated on more than one occasion is enough to prosecute it as a crime.

High Punishment: Lashed once with a whip for every offense and then 1 year imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Low Punishment: Banishment from the community

Tax Evasion

In most societies ruled by a government, officials usually set dues to be collected by the populace to pay for various goods and services that said government provides. Tax evasion is the crime of avoiding the payment of these taxes, usually by hiding the amount of money one makes from government officials and paying less than one should have or not paying any amount of their taxes.

High Punishment: Fine equal to 200% of previous evaded taxes and 1 year imprisonment for every 100 gp owed

Normal Punishment: Fine equal to total evaded taxes and 1 year imprisonment for every 500 gp owed

Low Punishment: Fine equal to total evaded taxes

Theft

Theft is the crime of stealing property from its rightful owner. This crime, though similar to robbery, assumes no threats or force in the robbery and so encompasses many subcategories of crime such as pickpocketing or stealing from a residence when the owner is unaware.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per 200 gp worth of goods stolen and a fine equal to 200% the value of those goods

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment per 200 gp worth of goods stolen and a fine equal to the total value of those goods

Low Punishment: A fine equal to the value of the stolen goods

Trespassing

Trespassing is the crime of entering someone’s property or land without express permission. In most instances, this is self-evident such as in the cases of locked homes or storefronts, but there are some areas outdoors which may be protected by the law as well. These outdoor areas are usually marked by boundaries such as fences or signs which make it obvious where one should not tread without breaking the law.

High Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Normal Punishment: 1 month in the pillory

Low Punishment: 20 gp fine paid to the property owner

Unlawful Dueling

In some territories, dueling is a perfectly legal activity, though there are usually restrictions in place as to who can duel, when they can do so, and in what locations. In many instances an official must be present to judge the duel and ensure that all proper procedures are followed for the duel to be considered legal.

High Punishment: Removal of the hands at the wrists

Normal Punishment: 1 year imprisonment

Low Punishment: 1 week in the pillory

Vandalism

Vandalism is the damage or destruction of property belonging to another person. This crime can have a wide range of offenses such as breaking a window, painting someone’s home without their consent, defacing their belongings, and more. As such, the punishment for the crime is usually proportional to the cost of repairs.

High Punishment: Fine equal to 200% the value of the vandalized property and 10 lashes with a whip

Normal Punishment: Fine equal to 200% the value of the vandalized property

Low Punishment: Fine equal to the value of the vandalized property
